newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian police out in force to stop protests.
newsitem.headline: Albanian police out in force to stop protests.

text.p: Security was tight in central Tirana on Thursday as police sought to head off a second day of protests by angry investors in a failed get-rich-quick pyramid scheme amid reports that the business's owner had been arrested.
Police were stationed along roads leading to the capital's main Skanderbeg Square, scene of anti-government demonstrations last year, and at key road junctions, eyewitnesses said.

Small groups of disappointed savers clustered in front of the western Tirana appartment of 30-year old Romany gypsy woman Maksude Kadema, know as Sude, whose failure to repay thousands of depositors sparked street battles with police on Wednesday.
"We are asking for our rights and for our money," a middle-aged woman said.
Albanian media reported that police had arrested Kadema and 18 other people on suspicion of embezzlement after she publicly acknowledged her company was bankrupt.
Protesters, keeping a late-night vigil at her home, said officers led her away shortly after midnight and carried off piles of documents.
No one at the Prosecutor's Office was immediately available for comment.

Demonstrations against the shaky pyramid schemes, which have lured savers in Europe's poorest country with promises of 200 percent returns over three months, have coincided with an opposition call for mass protests.

The opposition Socialists, reformed heirs to the communists that ruled for half a century, have accused President Sali Berisha's conservative Democratic Party of pushing Albania to the brink of economic collapse and turning a blind eye to the murky pyramid business.
Protesters and some newspapers echoed the sentiment. In a commentary the independent daily newspaper Koha Jone said the moment had come to mirror unrest in fellow Balkan states Serbia and Bulgaria.

"One would have thought the opposition would have learned a valuable lesson from the demonstrations in Belgrade and Sofia...but Berisha has learned more. Police violence has shown he will protect the squares with fanaticism," the paper added.

Local media reported that more than a dozen protesters were hurt in Wednesday's clashes and there were 29 arrests. Thousands of people took to the streets in Tirana and breakaway groups hurled stones at riot police armed with batons.

In the southwestern port of Vlore, home to many of the myriad schemes that have sprung up since the fall of communism in 1990, there were unconfirmed reports of large demonstrations and clashes with police.
The collapse of Sude's scheme followed the demise of a similar company late last year. Four others have suspended repayments to investors.
The International Monetary Fund and the World Bank have both expressed concern at the spread of the shemes but the government has been slow to act against them.
